title: Buses, Reliability, Availability and RAID
subtitle: How the parts talk, how long they last, and how disks are combined to survive failures.

references.title: Storage Systems
references.topics: Buses and connections; reliability, availability and dependability measures; RAID levels 0, 1, 5, 6 and 10

objectives: Describe the data, address and control buses and calculate bus bandwidth
Define reliability, availability, MTTF, MTBF and MTTR
Calculate availability and downtime per year
Compare RAID 0, 1, 5, 6 and 10 for capacity and fault tolerance
Choose a RAID level for a given scenario and justify it

steps.question: A server has 100 disks and each disk fails on average once in 114 years. How often does the server lose a disk?
clues: Many components make failures **frequent**, even if each part is reliable.
The answer is **redundancy**: store extra information so a failure loses nothing.
Parts also have to **talk** to each other: that is the job of buses.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: What a bus is

head: Part
Carries
Determines
rows: The address of the memory location or device wanted
How much can be addressed: n address lines reach 2ⁿ locations (32 lines: 4 GiB of bytes)
The data being read or written
Bytes per transfer: a 64-bit bus moves 8 bytes at a time
Read / write, clock, interrupt, bus request and grant signals
Who talks, when, and in which direction

steps.why: A bus is a shared set of wires connecting the CPU, memory and I/O devices; the three groups of lines each have a different job.
steps.real: Modern systems use fast point-to-point serial links (such as PCI Express) in place of wide shared buses, but the same ideas apply.

mistake.wrong: The address bus width equals the data bus width.
mistake.right: They are independent: the address width fixes capacity, the data width fixes bytes per transfer.

explainAgain.beginner: A road: the address lines are the street name, the data lines are the lanes, and the traffic signals are the control lines.

steps.title: Bus bandwidth

terms.t: bandwidth = width in bytes × transfers per second
terms.note: a 64-bit bus at 100 MHz with one transfer per cycle: 8 × 100 million = 800 MB/s
two transfers per clock cycle double the bandwidth: 1,600 MB/s

items: A **synchronous** bus uses a clock; an **asynchronous** bus uses handshake signals
Several devices may want the bus: **arbitration** decides who gets it
Longer buses and more devices lower the achievable clock rate

steps.why: Bandwidth limits how fast data can reach the CPU or leave a disk array.
steps.real: Memory buses, graphics links and storage links are rated by their bandwidth.

steps.title: Calculate: bus bandwidth

blocks.title: Bus bandwidth and address space
blocks.equation: bandwidth = bytes per transfer × clock × transfers per cycle

steps.why: 64 bits at 100 MHz with one transfer per cycle gives 800 MB/s; with DDR (2 transfers) 1,600 MB/s. 32 address lines reach 4 GiB.

steps.question: A 64-bit data bus runs at 100 MHz with one transfer per clock cycle. What is its bandwidth?

reveal.text: 64 bits = 8 bytes. 8 bytes × 100 million transfers per second = **800 MB/s**.

steps.result: With DDR it would be 1,600 MB/s.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each bus with its job.

pairs.b: Read, write, clock and handshake signals

steps.why: The three buses cooperate in every transfer.

steps.question: A system has 32 address lines. How many byte locations can it address?
feedback: 32 is the number of lines, not locations.

steps.title: Fault, error, failure

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: A flipped bit in a memory cell
A wrong value that results from a fault
The system no longer delivers its service

steps.why: Faults are unavoidable. Good design stops faults from becoming failures.
steps.real: ECC memory corrects single-bit errors before they can cause a failure.

steps.title: MTTF, MTTR and availability

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Continuity of service until a failure
Mean time to failure: average time of correct operation
Mean time to repair: average time to restore service
Mean time between failures = MTTF + MTTR
The fraction of time the service is working

steps.why: Availability depends on both how seldom it fails (MTTF) and how fast it is repaired (MTTR).
steps.real: Service providers state availability in "nines": 99.99% is called four nines.

mistake.right: A component that fails rarely but takes a week to repair can have poor availability.

steps.title: Calculate: availability and downtime
steps.why: MTTF 1,000 h and MTTR 1 h give 99.9%: about 8.75 hours of downtime a year. Cut the repair time to 6 minutes (0.1 h) and downtime falls by a factor of ten.

steps.question: MTTF is 1,000 hours and MTTR is 1 hour. What is the availability?
steps.result: That is roughly 8.75 hours of downtime a year.

steps.title: The nines
steps.why: Each extra nine cuts the allowed downtime by a factor of ten and costs much more to achieve.
steps.real: Banks and telephone networks aim for four or five nines.

steps.title: Calculate: many disks fail more often

blocks.title: Failures in a large array (no redundancy)
blocks.equation: array MTTF = disk MTTF ÷ number of disks

steps.why: A disk with a 1,000,000 hour MTTF (about 114 years) is very reliable, but 100 of them together fail on average every 10,000 hours: about every 417 days. The quoted MTTF is a manufacturer's figure and assumes independent failures.

steps.question: 100 disks each have an MTTF of 1,000,000 hours (about 114 years). About how often does some disk in the array fail?

reveal.text: Failure rates add: MTTF of the array = 1,000,000 ÷ 100 = 10,000 hours ≈ **417 days**. More parts mean more failures.

steps.result: This is why large storage systems need redundancy.

steps.statement: Availability depends on how quickly a failed component is repaired.
steps.why: Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR): a smaller MTTR raises it.

steps.title: Redundant arrays of independent disks

items: **RAID** combines several disks into one logical disk
**Striping**: consecutive blocks go to different disks, so they can be read in parallel (speed)
**Mirroring**: the same block is kept on two disks (redundancy)
**Parity**: an extra block that lets a lost block be rebuilt (cheaper redundancy)

steps.why: RAID turns many unreliable disks into one fast and (if designed so) fault-tolerant disk.
steps.real: Servers, NAS boxes and cloud storage use RAID or a similar idea (erasure coding).

steps.title: Parity: rebuild from the rest

head: Block
Value (binary)
Value
rows: P = D0 XOR D1 XOR D2

blocks.text: If the disk holding D1 fails: **D1 = D0 XOR D2 XOR P = 10 XOR 3 XOR 15 = 6**. XOR of all remaining blocks gives the lost one.

steps.why: One parity block protects any number of data blocks against the loss of any one of them.
steps.real: RAID 5 and RAID 6 spread the parity across all the disks.

explainAgain.beginner: Three numbers and their total: if one number is lost, total minus the others gives it back. XOR does this for bits.

steps.title: Try it: the five RAID levels

blocks.title: RAID levels
blocks.hint: Click a disk to fail it, and see whether the data survives. Note: the demo mirrors RAID 1 across all its disks; the classic RAID 1 is two disks.

steps.why: With 4 disks: RAID 0 loses data with any failure; RAID 5 survives one; RAID 6 survives any two; RAID 10 survives one failure per mirrored pair (disks 0 and 1 failing together loses data, disks 0 and 2 do not).

steps.title: Comparing the levels

head: Level
How it works
Capacity (N disks)
Survives
Small write cost
rows: 1 failure guaranteed; more if in different pairs

steps.why: Every level trades capacity, fault tolerance and write speed. There is no single best choice.
steps.real: RAID 0 has no redundancy at all, so by itself it is the least reliable option.

mistake.wrong: RAID is a replacement for backups.
mistake.right: RAID survives disk failures, not deletion, corruption, fire or a faulty controller. Keep backups.

deeper.text: RAID 5 small-write problem: updating one block needs 4 I/Os: read old data, read old parity, write new data, write new parity (new parity = old parity XOR old data XOR new data).

steps.question: Four disks in RAID 10: disks 0 and 1 are a mirrored pair, disks 2 and 3 are the other pair. Disks 0 and 2 fail. Is the data still available?
options: Yes: each pair still has one good disk

reveal.text: Each mirrored pair still has one working disk (1 and 3), so **all data survives**. If disks 0 and 1 had failed, the whole pair would be lost.

steps.result: That is why RAID 10 guarantees only one failure.

steps.question: Six 2 TB disks in RAID 6. How much usable capacity and how many failures survived?

reveal.text: RAID 6 uses two disks' worth of parity: (6 − 2) × 2 TB = **8 TB**, and survives **any two** failures.

steps.result: RAID 5 would give 10 TB but survive only one failure.

steps.title: Calculate: rebuild time and capacity

blocks.title: Capacity and rebuild window
blocks.equation: Rebuild time = disk size ÷ rebuild rate (illustrative)

steps.why: Six 2 TB disks: 12, 10, 8 and 6 TB. Rebuilding a 4 TB disk at 100 MB/s takes 11.1 hours, during which RAID 5 cannot survive another failure: one reason RAID 6 is preferred for big disks.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about RAID is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. RAID 0 improves speed but gives no fault tolerance.
2. RAID 5 survives the failure of any one disk.
3. RAID 6 stores two parity blocks per stripe.
4. RAID 1 doubles the usable capacity of the disks.
steps.explain: Mirroring halves the usable capacity: every block is stored twice.
steps.fix: RAID 1 uses half the capacity for the copy.

steps.title: The scenario

blocks.text: **You are designing storage for a banking database. Which RAID configuration would you choose and why?**

items: **Write performance**: banking databases do many small random writes
**Availability**: the system must stay up through a disk failure and its repair
**Recovery**: protection against more than disk failure

steps.why: The right answer follows from the requirements, not from a rule: first list what matters, then compare the levels.
steps.real: Real designs combine RAID with hot spares, battery-backed write caches, replication to another site and regular backups.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Which RAID level would you pick for the banking database, and what would you say to someone who suggests RAID 5 to save money?
ideas: RAID 10: best write performance and fastest rebuild; survives a failure in each mirrored pair; the cost is 50% capacity.
RAID 5 has the 4-I/O small-write penalty, which hurts a transaction workload.
RAID 5 rebuilds are long and a second failure during the rebuild loses the data; RAID 6 would be safer if capacity matters more.
RAID is not a backup: add replication and off-site backups.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: A colleague says "RAID 6 means we do not need backups". What do you answer?
steps.answer: RAID protects against disk failure only. Accidental deletion, software bugs, ransomware, a controller fault, fire or theft affect all the disks at once or are copied to every disk. Backups (preferably off-site) protect against those cases, so RAID and backups serve different purposes.

steps.question: For a write-heavy transaction database, which is the usual choice?
steps.why: Mirrored stripes give fast writes and good fault tolerance.
feedback: RAID 5 has the small-write penalty and a vulnerable rebuild.
One failure would lose the data.

questions.a: Both MTTF (how rarely it fails) and MTTR (how fast it is repaired).

questions.q: How does parity let a lost block be rebuilt?
questions.a: XOR the remaining blocks and the parity.

questions.q: Why is RAID not a backup?
questions.a: It protects against disk failure only, not deletion, corruption or site loss.

steps.question: Name the three buses and what each carries.
steps.answer: Address bus (the location wanted), data bus (the data) and control bus (read/write, clock, handshake).
steps.solution: Each group of lines has a distinct job.

steps.question: MTTF 1,000 hours, MTTR 1 hour. Find the availability and the downtime per year.
Data blocks 10, 6 and 3 are protected by an XOR parity block. Find the parity and rebuild the lost block 6.
A 128-bit bus runs at 200 MHz with two transfers per cycle. Find its bandwidth, and the address space if it has 36 address lines.
steps.solution: 16 bytes × 200 million cycles × 2 = 6,400 MB/s. 2³⁶ bytes = 64 GiB.

steps.question: A disk has an MTTF of 1,000,000 hours. An array has 100 such disks without redundancy. Find the array MTTF in hours and days. If repair takes 24 hours, what is the availability of one disk?
steps.title: Exam practice: array failures

steps.question: Four disks in RAID 5, RAID 6 and RAID 10 (pairs 0-1 and 2-3). Which survive (a) disks 0 and 1 failing, (b) disks 0 and 2 failing?
steps.solution: RAID 5 survives one failure. RAID 6 survives any two. RAID 10 survives if no mirrored pair loses both disks: 0 and 1 are a pair (lost), 0 and 2 are in different pairs (safe).
steps.mistake: Assuming RAID 10 survives any two failures.
steps.title: Exam practice: survival

steps.question: Eight 4 TB disks. Give the usable capacity for RAID 0, 5, 6 and 10, and the number of failures each is guaranteed to survive.
steps.answer: RAID 0: 32 TB, 0. RAID 5: 28 TB, 1. RAID 6: 24 TB, 2. RAID 10: 16 TB, 1.
steps.solution: RAID 0 uses all 8 disks; RAID 5 loses one disk's worth to parity; RAID 6 loses two; RAID 10 stores every block twice.
steps.title: Exam practice: capacity

steps.question: You are designing storage for a banking database. Which RAID configuration would you choose and why?
steps.answer: RAID 10 for the transaction database: it gives the best write performance (no parity small-write penalty), fast rebuilds and tolerates a failure in each mirrored pair, at the price of 50% capacity. RAID 6 could serve large read-mostly archives where capacity matters more. In both cases add hot spares, a battery-backed cache, replication or off-site backups, because RAID does not protect against deletion or site loss.
steps.solution: A strong answer weighs reliability, write performance, capacity, cost and rebuild risk, and mentions backups.
steps.mistake: Choosing RAID 0 for speed, or saying RAID replaces backups.
steps.title: Exam practice: banking database
What you should remember
remember: A bus has address, data and control lines; bandwidth = bytes per transfer × transfers per second.
Availability = MTTF ÷ (MTTF + MTTR); each extra nine cuts downtime tenfold.
More components mean more failures: array MTTF = disk MTTF ÷ number of disks.
RAID 0 stripes (no redundancy); RAID 1 and 10 mirror; RAID 5 and 6 use one or two parity blocks.
Parity is the XOR of the data blocks; XOR of the rest rebuilds a lost block.
Choose the level from the requirements and keep backups.

mistakes.right: It protects only against disk failure.
Only if the failures are in different mirrored pairs.
It has no redundancy at all.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: Buses carry addresses, data and control signals, and their bandwidth is width times transfer rate. Large systems fail often, so reliability is measured by MTTF and MTTR and availability by MTTF divided by MTTF + MTTR. RAID combines striping, mirroring and parity: RAID 0 for speed, RAID 1 and 10 for mirrored redundancy, RAID 5 and 6 for parity with one or two failures tolerated. The choice depends on the requirements, and backups are still needed.
